President Donald Trump on Tuesday told reporters he would deploy National Guard troops to Chicago but didn't say when.
"Well, we're going in," Trump said in the Oval Office when asked if he's made a decision on the matter after days of threats and warnings.
"Look, I have an obligation.
This isn't a political thing.
I have an obligation," Trump said.

President Donald Trump listens to a question during an event to announce that the Space Force Command will move from Colorado to Alabama, in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, September 2, 2025.
Trump pointed to gun violence in the city over Labor Day weekend as a reason for federal intervention.
He said Illinois Gov.
JB Pritzker, a Democrat, should be requesting his administration's help.
"If the governor of Illinois would call up, call me up, I would love to do it.
Now, we're going to do it anyway.
We have the right to do it because I have an obligation to protect this country," Trump said.
Pritzker quickly pushed back as he and other Chicago officials held a news conference on Tuesday afternoon.
"First, I want to address the president's unhinged remarks a few minutes ago begging me to call him.
No, I will not call the president, asking him to send troops to Chicago.
I've made that clear already," Pritzker said.
Pritzker, Chicago's Democratic Mayor Brandon Johnson and various local officials rejected Trump's desire to send National Guard troops to the city.
They emphasized there is no "emergency" unfolding in Chicago that would justify such a move, with Pritzker saying it's all "a big show" on Trump's part.
"When did we become a country where it's okay for the U.S. president to insist on national television that a state should call him to beg for anything, especially something we don't want.
Have we truly lost all sense of sanity in this nation, that we treat this as normal?" Pritzker said.

A U.S. official confirmed to ABC News last month that planning was underway at the Pentagon for the potential use of National Guard troops in Chicago -- an area Trump has repeatedly singled out as he mulled sending the Guard to other major American cities following his federal takeover of Washington.
Trump then appeared to back off somewhat, saying he preferred cities ask for his administration's assistance.
On Monday, Mayor Johnson led a chant of "no troops in Chicago" at a Labor Day march.
Earlier Tuesday, Trump ramped up the threats.
Violent crime in Chicago dropped significantly in the first half of the year, according to official data released by the city.
Shootings were down 37% and homicides have dropped by 32% compared to the first half of 2024, while total violence crime dropped by over 22%, according to the crime statistics.

Meanwhile, the administration is preparing for a surge in increased immigration enforcement operations in Chicago as soon as this week, sources told ABC News.
Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said the intention was for more resources to be sent to Chicago but did not divulge details.
Pritzker said he expected Chicago to experience something similar to what played out in Los Angeles and Washington, including the positioning of armed federal agents on federal property.
"Let's be clear, the terror and cruelty is the point, not the safety of anyone living here," Pritzker said.
